workingTitle: A less stable molecule outnumbers its sturdier twin in interstellar space
freshness: Astronomy & Astrophysics-accepted paper posted to arXiv on October 29, 2026; selected within the preferred 15-day window.
coreFacts: The team reports the first interstellar detection of O-protonated isocyanic acid, HNCOH+, toward Galactic Center molecular cloud G+0.693-0.027.
An ultra-deep survey with the Yebes 40-meter, IRAM 30-meter, and APEX telescopes covered nearly 150 GHz between 31 and 275 GHz.

The survey covered eight predicted rotational transitions; four fell in frequency gaps and one was excluded because of atmospheric blending, while a nearly complete remaining progression supported the identification.
The fitted column density is (9.9 +/- 0.5) x 10^12 molecules per square centimeter and the abundance relative to molecular hydrogen is 7.3(+1.3/-1.0) x 10^-11.
HNCOH+ is 3.8(+0.5/-0.4) times as abundant as the more thermodynamically stable H2NCO+ isomer in this cloud.
The abundance ratio agrees with kinetic calculations in which protonation of HNCO preferentially forms HNCOH+, showing that reaction rates can dominate over equilibrium stability.
caveats: The detected ion contains the isocyanate functional group found within peptide bonds, but it is not a peptide, protein, organism, or evidence of life.
Most millimeter-wave transition frequencies were extrapolated from limited laboratory microwave measurements; the authors call for targeted laboratory spectroscopy.
The result measures one chemically rich Galactic Center cloud and does not establish that the same abundance ratio holds throughout the interstellar medium.
